passage: I am Rekha, and I still remember the corridor of the junior hostel in my first month. Imran, a final-year senior, lined up the four of us and told us to make a shy new junior, Dev, stand on a chair and sing until told to stop. He called it tradition. I laughed louder than anyone so that nobody would pick me next. Dev's hands shook. Nisha looked at the floor. Aakash shook his head very slightly but said nothing. I told myself it was Imran's order, so it was Imran's doing, not mine. I felt lighter for about an hour. Later I could not remember Dev's song, only Dev's face.

qa.q: What did Imran tell the four juniors to make Dev do?
qa.a: Imran told them to make Dev stand on a chair and sing until told to stop.

qa.q: Why did Rekha laugh louder than anyone in the corridor?
qa.a: Rekha was afraid of being picked next, and comforted by the thought that it was Imran's order, not Rekha's doing; the lighter feeling lasted only about an hour before guilt came.

qa.q: What choice in the corridor could have protected Dev?
qa.a: Rekha could have refused to laugh, stepped away, or told the warden or a trusted teacher afterwards; one person disagreeing shows the others they do not have to join in.

qa.q: How might Dev have experienced that evening?
qa.a: Dev's shaking hands suggest fear and humiliation, with no sign that anyone would stand up for Dev.

grounding: A new junior does what a senior demands to avoid punishment, treating the senior as responsible, which is how harm gets done.

passage: Supervisor's note, intern week three. Deepak was told by Payal, a senior analyst, to enter the client figures again using her login because the deadline was close. He did, and when I asked, he said, "Payal said it was fine." Two other interns watched and said nothing. I spoke with Deepak privately that afternoon: nobody had threatened him, but he feared a bad reference. I told him it is fine to ask "is this okay?" and that using someone else's login is against our rules, whoever asks. I reported it to the office manager the same day, and I will speak to Payal tomorrow. — Nikhil, floor supervisor

qa.q: Whose login did Deepak use to enter the figures?
qa.a: Deepak used Payal's login to enter the client figures again.

qa.q: Why did Deepak say "Payal said it was fine" when Nikhil asked?
qa.a: Deepak was moving responsibility onto the senior analyst and felt anxious about a bad reference, which is why he complied without asking.

qa.q: What turning point in Nikhil's private talk could help Deepak next time?
qa.a: Nikhil told Deepak it is fine to ask "is this okay?" and that the rule applies whoever asks, which gives Deepak words to use and takes away the fear of asking.

qa.q: How might Payal see the situation?
qa.a: Payal may have been under deadline pressure and thought of the shortcut as small, without noticing how a new intern would feel unable to say no.

grounding: A new intern does what a senior instructs to gain favour or avoid trouble, feeling that responsibility has moved to the person giving the order.

passage:
I'm Pranav, and my first month as an intern at the city newspaper still makes me wince.
Elizabeth, the senior reporter, was a legend on our floor. Everyone wanted her to notice them. One evening she handed me a note. “Put this quote from the shop owners' association in the market story. No need to call them. I've got it covered.”
The other interns were watching. I didn't call. I typed it in, and in my head the thought was clear: this is her call, not mine.
The quote was wrong. It named a small sweet shop as the one selling stale stock. The owner came to the office two days later, holding the paper, shaking.
Elizabeth shrugged. I couldn't. My name was on that story too.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth tell Pranav not to do?
qa.a: She told him there was no need to call the shop owners' association.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when the sweet shop owner came in?
qa.a: Pranav felt ashamed and guilty; he couldn't shrug it off because his name was on the story too.

qa.q: What could Pranav have done that evening instead?
qa.a: Pranav could have made the quick call anyway, or told Elizabeth that checking felt right, since checking was still Pranav's responsibility.

qa.q: How might the sweet shop owner have experienced the story?
qa.a: The owner was likely frightened and upset about losing customers because of a false quote, which is why the owner came in shaking.

grounding: An intern follows a senior's instruction to gain favour, feeling the responsibility belongs to the senior, and harm follows.

passage:
Warden's note, Girls' Hostel Block C, Wednesday night.
At about 11 pm I heard raised voices on the second floor. Rashmi, a third-year, was standing in the corridor with four seniors. Sunaina, a second-year, had locked the common-room door with a first-year inside the dark room, calling it punishment for “not greeting properly”.
When I asked Sunaina, she said, “Rashmi di told me to. I just did what I was told.” She could not look at me. The first-year was crying but unhurt.
I opened the door at once, sat with the first-year until she was calm, and called the anti-ragging committee convenor the same night. Rashmi and Sunaina will meet the committee tomorrow. I have told the first-year she did nothing wrong.

qa.q: What reason was given for locking the first-year in the common room?
qa.a: It was called punishment for "not greeting properly".

qa.q: What did Sunaina's not looking at the warden suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt ashamed and guilty, even while telling herself she only did what Rashmi told her.

qa.q: What steps did the warden take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: The warden opened the door at once, stayed with the first-year, told her it wasn't her fault and called the anti-ragging convenor that night, which protected her and made the seniors accountable.

qa.q: How might the first-year have felt inside the dark room?
qa.a: She was probably terrified and humiliated, alone in the dark and unsure when it would end.

grounding: A warden's note shows a junior obeying a senior's ragging order and passing responsibility up to the one who gave it, which is how harm is done.

passage:
Thursday, 11 pm
Dilnaz ma'am told me again today to tell the tailor, Bhola bhai, that his payment for the wedding costumes was processed. It isn't. It's stuck because the client hasn't paid us.
“Just say it's processed. I'll handle the rest,” she said. Rohit and Neha, the other interns, nodded at me like, do it, she's the boss.
So I called and said it. Bhola bhai said, “Thank you, beta, I'll tell my workers they'll get their wages Saturday.”
I keep telling myself: her order, her problem. I'm only an intern. But I'm the one who said the words. I'm the one his workers will be waiting on.
Tomorrow I'll ask ma'am if I can at least tell him the real date.
— Yogesh

qa.q: What was Yogesh told to tell Bhola bhai?
qa.a: He was told to say that his payment for the wedding costumes was processed.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after the call?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uneasy; he keeps telling himself it's ma'am's problem, but he knows he said the words.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do next, and who could help?
qa.a: He could ask Dilnaz ma'am to let him tell Bhola bhai the real date, and if she refuses, raise it with the company head rather than repeat the lie.

qa.q: How might Bhola bhai's workers be affected?
qa.a: They are expecting their wages on Saturday, so they may be left short and disappointed because of a false promise.

grounding: An intern follows a senior's instruction to avoid trouble, telling himself responsibility is hers, and real harm follows.

passage:
Seniors' group, 11:52 pm
Chinmay: Trisha, get the 4 new ones from room 214 into the corridor. intro session. now.
Trisha: ok bhaiya, on it
Trisha to Megha, 11:54 pm
Megha: are you seriously knocking on their doors at midnight??
Trisha: Chinmay said. not my call
Trisha: if anything goes wrong it's on him, not me
Megha: you're the one knocking though
Trisha: he's final year. if I say no, I'm the one getting "introduced" next week
Megha: that's exactly how this keeps going. this is ragging, Trisha
Megha: I've messaged Warden ma'am
Warden ma'am to Megha, 11:58 pm
Warden ma'am: Thank you for telling me. I'm coming up to the second floor now. Nobody needs to stand in the corridor. Please stay in your rooms.
Trisha to Megha, 11:59 pm
Trisha: she's coming up. I hadn't knocked yet
Trisha: I think I was going to, though

qa.q: How many new students did Chinmay tell Trisha to bring into the corridor?
qa.a: The 4 new ones from room 214.

qa.q: What is Trisha afraid of if Trisha refuses Chinmay?
qa.a: Trisha is scared of being the next one "introduced", and eases the guilt by treating the whole thing as Chinmay's responsibility.

qa.q: What went wrong in Trisha's thinking, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Trisha treated the order as moving the blame to Chinmay; refusing and telling the warden, as Megha did, keeps each person responsible for what they do.

qa.q: What would it have been like for the four new students if Trisha had knocked?
qa.a: They would likely have felt frightened and humiliated, woken at midnight and made to stand in a corridor, whoever gave the order.

grounding: Shows a junior obeying a senior's ragging order and feeling the responsibility belongs to the senior, which is how harm gets done, with a peer and the warden stopping it.
